Part 8 of Block Diffusion RooflinesPrevious: 7 · Worked examplesNext: 9 · The measurement stack

Proposition 1 takes two kinds of input that Parts 1–7 do not measure: the rates of the accelerator, taken from its datasheet, and the experts each pass touches, taken from the assumption that tokens route independently (A2). This chapter measures both on one H200, for DiffusionGemma and Gemma 4, and shows that routing is the input that moves the bound most, in opposite directions at small and at large batch.

What one H200 sustains

The datasheet rates of an H200 (989 TFLOP/s in BF16, 1,979 in FP8, 4.8 TB/s) assume its 1,980 MHz boost clock and say nothing about attention. A kernel that keeps the tensor cores busy draws power until it reaches the 700 W cap, and the GPU then lowers its clock. The rates a kernel can reach are therefore measured, in the manner of the Empirical Roofline Toolkit: one benchmark per rate, with the clock and the power logged during each.

Definition 5Empirical ceilings and empirical roofline

In short. The empirical ceiling of a rate is the highest value measured on this GPU; the empirical roofline of a component is \(\max(F_c/\hat\pi_c,\ Q_c/\hat\beta)\) at those ceilings.

The empirical ceiling of a rate is the highest value that its benchmarks reach on random data:

  • \(\hat\pi_{\mathrm{fp8}}\), \(\hat\pi_{\mathrm{bf16}}\): GEMMs of 11 shapes from \(2048^3\) to \(32768 \times 4096 \times 4096\), each run for 0.5 s, a short burst of an \(8192^3\) GEMM, and the model's own projections at 1 to 16,384 tokens, replayed from CUDA graphs in bursts of about 2 ms;
  • \(\hat\pi_{\mathrm{attn}}\): FlashAttention 3 at head dimension 128 on long square sequences, sustained for 0.5 s. Attention kernels at other shapes can exceed it in short bursts (up to 729 TFLOP/s for FlashAttention 4 at head dimension 256 on TD's rows), so for attention the ceiling is a sustained reference rate rather than a maximum;
  • \(\hat\beta\): reads and copies of 0.25–8 GB buffers.

A component \(c\) of a pass (experts, dense GEMMs, window attention, global attention, vocabulary head) with \(F_c\) FLOPs and \(Q_c\) bytes of memory traffic has the empirical roofline

\[ \tau_c = \max\Bigl(\frac{F_c}{\hat\pi_c},\ \frac{Q_c}{\hat\beta}\Bigr), \]

with \(\hat\pi_c\) the ceiling of its kind: FP8 GEMM for dense layers and experts, attention for attention, BF16 GEMM for the vocabulary head. The empirical roofline of a pass is \(\tau = \sum_c \tau_c\), the kernel-by-kernel rule of Part 5.

The measured roofline sits below the datasheet's, more in compute than in bandwidth.

Attainable throughput \(\min(\pi, I\beta)\) against arithmetic intensity, log–log, for FP8 linear layers. Dashed: datasheet (1,979 TFLOP/s, 4.8 TB/s). Solid orange: empirical ceilings of Table 11. Blue: the attention ceiling, which applies to attention kernels whatever their intensity. The ridge point, where a kernel turns compute-bound, moves from 412 to 340 FLOP/byte.

Three findings set how the ceilings are used.

  • Power, not the tensor cores, limits sustained compute. On random data, GEMMs that run for half a second hold 1,300–1,500 MHz at 690 W: 700 TFLOP/s in BF16 and 1,336 in FP8. Per clock cycle the BF16 rate is 0.93 of the datasheet's, so the kernels are close to ideal and the shortfall is the clock. On constant inputs, whose bits do not toggle, the same GEMMs draw about 450 W and run 20% faster. Kernels inside the engine run for milliseconds between memory-bound kernels and see higher clocks, which is why the ceiling is the highest rate measured, including the 2 ms bursts.
  • Attention has its own ceiling. FlashAttention 3 sustains 638 TFLOP/s, 13% below a BF16 GEMM at the same clock: the softmax between its two matrix products costs that much.
  • Small GEMMs are bound by latency. With 64 tokens or fewer, the model's projections take 5–12 µs whatever the batch and stream their weights at 1–3 TB/s, below \(\hat\beta\). This is the floor of an AR step at small batch; neither of the two GEMM libraries tested at these shapes, cuBLAS and vLLM's CUTLASS kernels, does better.

In particular, the empirical ceilings lower compute (0.74 of the datasheet in FP8) more than bandwidth (0.90). They therefore barely change \(\Gamma\) where both decoders are memory-bound, and lower it where TD is compute-bound and AR is not.

Which experts a pass touches

The expert weights a pass reads, and hence the MoE penalty of Part 3, depend on how many distinct experts its tokens select. Assumption A2 of Proposition 1 takes the tokens to choose independently and uniformly, so that \(N\) tokens touch \(U_{E,k}(N) = E\,[1 - (1 - k/E)^N]\) of the \(E = 128\) experts of a layer, each token selecting \(k = 8\). A canvas of 256 positions then touches all 128 experts even at batch 1. The router's choices can be counted directly: the engine records, for every pass and MoE layer, how many tokens went to each expert.

Definition 6Measured routing

In short. \(U^{\mathrm{meas}}\) counts the experts a pass actually touches; \(U^{\mathrm{freq}}\) is what independent tokens with the measured popularity would touch; \(N^{\mathrm{eff}}\) is the number of uniformly routed tokens that would touch \(U^{\mathrm{meas}}\).

A pass holds \(N\) tokens: \(N = B\) for an AR step and \(N = Bb\) for a TD pass. For a decoder at batch \(B\) and context \(C\):

  • \(U^{\mathrm{meas}}\) is the number of distinct experts a pass touches in one MoE layer, averaged over the 30 layers and the timed passes; across the three repeats of a point, its median.
  • \(\rho_e\) is the probability that a token selects expert \(e\), estimated per layer from all passes of a run, and \(U^{\mathrm{freq}} = \sum_{e=1}^{E} \bigl[1 - (1 - \rho_e)^N\bigr]\) is the count that \(N\) independent tokens with these frequencies would touch. The term \((1 - \rho_e)^N\) is estimated without bias from the run's counts.
  • \(N^{\mathrm{eff}}\), the effective number of independent tokens, solves \(U_{E,k}(N^{\mathrm{eff}}) = U^{\mathrm{meas}}\): the number of tokens that, routed independently and uniformly, would touch as many experts as the pass does.

Then \(U^{\mathrm{freq}}/U_{E,k}(N)\) measures the effect of uneven expert popularity, and \(U^{\mathrm{meas}}/U^{\mathrm{freq}}\) the effect of dependence between the tokens of a pass.

The two decoders depart from A2 in different ways. All counts below are from essay prompts (Part 9); at context 64k fewer than half of TD's measured canvases are ordinary text (Part 11), so the 64k counts for TD are the least representative.

  • AR is independent once popularity is counted. \(U^{\mathrm{meas}}/U^{\mathrm{freq}}\) is 0.98–1.03 at every point, while popularity alone removes 35–49% of the experts that uniform routing predicts from batch 8 on: at batch 64 and context 4k, independent tokens with the measured popularity touch 69 experts, the measured count is 69, and uniform routing predicts 126.
  • TD's experts are also unevenly popular, and its positions are dependent. Popularity removes 7–36% of the uniform count for a canvas (\(U^{\mathrm{freq}}\) is 82–119 of 128 at contexts 1k–16k). On top of it, \(U^{\mathrm{meas}}/U^{\mathrm{freq}}\) is 0.76–0.86 at batch 1 and 0.81–0.98 from batch 2 on, at contexts 1k–16k. Per layer the dependence is strongest in the first five MoE layers, which hold the lowest ratio at 23 of 25 points (0.49 in the first layer at batch 1 and 1k, against 0.82 on average over layers 6–30).
  • Context barely moves TD's count up to 16k. At batch 16, \(U^{\mathrm{meas}}\) is 104, 106 and 107 at 1k, 4k and 16k, and 84 at 64k, where the generated text degrades.

In particular, at batch 1 a canvas of 256 positions touches 64–74 experts per layer at contexts 1k–16k, as many as 11 to 13 independent tokens, and at batch 64 its 16,384 positions touch as many as 38. An AR step at batch 64 touches as many as 12 independent tokens: its sequences are independent, but the popular experts take most of the selections. The DiffusionGemma technical report counts about 84 experts per canvas on PG-19 with its adaptive sampler, about 17 independent tokens, which is within the range of the batch-1 repeats here (32–79 experts at 1k–16k).

Remark 3Proposition 1 at measured routing

In short. Measured routing enters Proposition 1 only through the expert penalty, which becomes \(U^{\mathrm{meas}}_{TD}/U^{\mathrm{meas}}_{AR}\).

Proposition 1 depends on routing only through the expert weights that a pass reads, \(s_wL\,U\,W^e\) bytes for \(L\) MoE layers of \(W^e\) parameters per expert. Replacing A2 by the measured counts therefore amounts to replacing \(N\) by \(N^{\mathrm{eff}}\) in the weights of both decoders, \(\class{mj-ar}{W_{AR}}(B)\) with \(U^{\mathrm{meas}}_{AR}\) experts per layer and \(\class{mj-td}{W_{TD}}(B)\) with \(U^{\mathrm{meas}}_{TD}\). In particular the expert penalty of Proposition 3 becomes

\[ \Pi_E = \frac{U_{E,k}(N^{\mathrm{eff}}_{TD})}{U_{E,k}(N^{\mathrm{eff}}_{AR})} = \frac{U^{\mathrm{meas}}_{TD}}{U^{\mathrm{meas}}_{AR}}, \]

and AR's linear intensity \(I_{\mathrm{lin}}(B) = 2BN_{\mathrm{act}}/(s_w\class{mj-ar}{W_{AR}}(B))\) changes with it, and so do the expert share \(\theta_E\), the parity batch and every threshold of Parts 3–5 that depends on \(\class{mj-ar}{W_{AR}}\). The FLOPs, the KV-cache bytes and the ceilings are unchanged.

At batch 1 and context 1k the measured routing lowers the linear penalty from 7.9 to 4.3, and Proposition 1 then gives \(\Gamma = 4.2\), against 2.3 under A2 (Proposition 1 without the vocabulary; the exact accounting of map (b) gives 2.7) and 7.0 measured; the measured gain is higher still because TD runs closer to its roofline than AR there (Part 11). From batch 8 on, at contexts 1k–16k, the measured penalty is higher than under A2 (1.85 against 1.13 at batch 32), because AR's count (33–71 experts at batch 8–64 and contexts 1k–4k) falls further below A2's prediction (52–126) than TD's (97–117 against 128). Proposition 1 then overestimates the gain (2.0 against a measured 1.04 at batch 32): it leaves out the vocabulary head, which TD evaluates at all 256 positions of every pass; the head, the sampler and self-conditioning together take 24–34% of TD's step at contexts of 1k–4k from batch 4 on.

The bound at measured inputs

The exact accounting includes the vocabulary head, activations and the KV cache. Evaluated pass by pass at each measured point, with the kernel-by-kernel rule, it gives the bound at the book's assumptions and at each measured input in turn.

Figure 23

The gain bound moves with each measured input, and routing moves it most.

Map

Roofline bound on \(\Gamma\) over batch \(B\) and context \(C\), with FP8 weights. Each map changes one input of the previous one. Orange: TD faster; blue: AR faster; the shade grows with \(|\log\Gamma|\) on one scale shared by Figures 23 and 33. Missing cells were not measured: the grid keeps \(BC \le 2^{21}\) tokens, and TD's batches at \((32, 64\text{k})\) and \((64, 16\text{k})\) did not fit in memory.

  • Ceilings, (a) to (b). At batch 1 the gain bound keeps 0.88–0.97 of its value, lowest at 64k. From batch 8 on, where TD is compute-bound and AR is not, it keeps 0.76–0.88.
  • Routing, (b) to (c). At batch 1 the bound rises by a factor 1.4–1.6; from batch 32 on it falls to 0.68–0.78 of (b). At contexts 1k–4k the batch at which AR overtakes TD moves from beyond 64 to between 32 and 64, and up to 16k the bound now falls with the batch from batch 1, where under A2 with datasheet rates, map (a), it rose up to batch 4–8.

Routing is therefore the input that moves the bound most, and it moves it in both directions: at small batch a canvas touches fewer experts than A2 predicts, which favours TD, and at large batch the uneven popularity of experts lowers AR's count further than TD's, which favours AR. Part 11 compares the bound (c) with the measured gain.
